batch_name: Kenelm Digby, Samuel Hartlib, and the London Chymical Networks
description: Events from Betty Jo Dobbs, 'Studies in the Natural Philosophy of Sir Kenelm Digby Part II: Digby and Alchemy' (Ambix, 1973). Documents Digby's alchemical activities at Gresham College (1633-35), Winchester House (1642-44), Paris exile (1644-1660), and his connections to the Hartlib circle and the early Royal Society.

persons.name: Samuel Hartlib
persons.bio_html:
Samuel Hartlib (c. 1600–1662) was a Prussian-born English educational reformer, intelligencer, and patron of natural philosophy who served as the central node of a vast correspondence network connecting natural philosophers, alchemists, chemical physicians, and reformers across England and Europe in the middle decades of the seventeenth century. Betty Jo Dobbs, in her study of Kenelm Digby and alchemy (Ambix, 1973), describes Hartlib as 'primarily interested in educational and religious reform but was perhaps more socially and practically oriented than many reformers,' who 'undertook to be a sort of communications centre for the collection and dissemination of information of all sorts' and attempted unsuccessfully to institutionalize this role as a state-supported Office of Address. He entered England as a student in 1625 and by the 1640s had built up a correspondence that included men of every intellectual persuasion; his daybook (the 'Ephemerides,' 1634–1660) records chemical references as early as 1640. Among his close chemical associates were Robert Boyle, George Starkey, Frederick Clodius (who married Hartlib's daughter and set up a laboratory in Hartlib's back kitchen), and Sir Kenelm Digby. Hartlib maintained contact with Continental chemical developments through the chemist-divine Johann Moriaen in Holland.

Hartlib's circle hoped that Boyle and Starkey would achieve major breakthroughs in chemical medicine and alchemy through the 1640s and early 1650s, but Hartlib's faith in Starkey declined sharply by 1653–4, while his hopes transferred to Frederick Clodius and later Digby. Hartlib corresponded with the Royal Society's first Secretary, Henry Oldenburg, who was the son-in-law of Hartlib's co-worker John Dury and who after Hartlib's death converted Hartlib's correspondence model into the public format of the Philosophical Transactions (1665). Hartlib's extensive papers — which include inventories of Digby's Gresham College laboratory, records of alchemical processes, correspondence with Boyle, and a daybook tracking developments in chemistry, alchemy, husbandry, and educational reform — are preserved at Sheffield University.

events.title: Kenelm Digby Establishes Alchemical Laboratory at Gresham College
events.description: Following the death of his wife Venetia in 1633, Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665) withdrew from public life for approximately two years and 'diverted himselfe with his chymistry, and the professors' good conversation' at Gresham College in London. Betty Jo Dobbs, in Ambix (1973), reconstructs the period from John Aubrey's brief lives and Digby's own later recollections: Digby had at Gresham 'a fair and large Laboratory... erected under the Lodgings of the Divinity-Reader' and his lodgings were 'at the end of your great Gallery.' An inventory of the laboratory's contents, dated 1 August 1648 and preserved in the Hartlib Papers at Sheffield University, lists a substantial and technically sophisticated installation across multiple rooms: a great glass case with several large glasses, an anatomy board with drawers, a drying oven, an oven with iron retorts, a deliquum stone and cellar, a reverberating calcining oven, a balneum mariae (water bath), sand and retort furnaces, a furnace for retorts in open fire, an athanor or digestive furnace, twenty alembic bodies of several sizes, glass basins, glass funnels, iron trivets, earthenware vessels, a water cistern, grinding stones of speckled marble, a large screw press, stone mortars, and three vaporatories. During this period Digby employed the Hungarian laboratory operator Johannes Banfi Hunnyades (1576–1650), who arrived in England in 1632 and became a favourite among gentlemen alchemists; Digby also conducted experiments on palingenesis, attempting to revivify plants and animals from their calcined ashes — including successful experiments with calcined crayfishes.
events.scholarly_grounding: Betty Jo Dobbs reconstructed Digby's Gresham College activities from Aubrey's Lives, Digby's own Of the Vegetation of Plants (1660/1669), and the Hartlib Papers laboratory inventory in 'Studies in the Natural Philosophy of Sir Kenelm Digby Part II: Digby and Alchemy' in Ambix vol. 20 no. 3 (1973) pp.143-163.

events.title: Digby Conducts Alchemy at Winchester House During Parliamentary Imprisonment
events.description: In 1642 Parliament imprisoned Sir Kenelm Digby — a Catholic Royalist — at Winchester House, the former episcopal palace of Lancelot Andrewes. Betty Jo Dobbs, in Ambix (1973), reconstructs his activities there from Longueville's Life (1896) and other sources: Digby 'established a laboratory for himself and hired a worker from a nearby glass factory, John Colnett, to be his operator.' The fruit of this collaboration was an improved method for manufacturing glass bottles, stronger than the commercially available glassware of the period, whose defects 'negated many experimental results, even when the glasses did not break at a crucial point.' Digby's invention came to light only in 1662 when Colnett applied for a patent on the process and was opposed by workers who knew the process to have been Digby's; the petitioners against Colnett's patent told the Attorney-General that 'Sir Kenlem first invented glass bottles nearly thirty years since' — placing the activity ca. 1633–5, possibly at Gresham College rather than Winchester House. After being released following petitions by influential friends, Digby went into exile in France (1644), where he lived principally until the Restoration in 1660. The Winchester House period represents the second of Digby's three major phases of chemical and alchemical activity, and the glassware invention demonstrates his empirical orientation toward improving the material conditions of experimental research.
events.scholarly_grounding: Betty Jo Dobbs documented Digby's Winchester House imprisonment and glass bottle work in 'Studies in the Natural Philosophy of Sir Kenelm Digby Part II: Digby and Alchemy' in Ambix vol. 20 no. 3 (1973) pp.143-163, citing Longueville and patent records.

events.title: John Evelyn Visits Digby in Paris: Exchange of Alchemical Preparations
events.description: In November 1651 the diarist John Evelyn visited Sir Kenelm Digby in Paris and the two men exchanged chemical preparations, as Evelyn recorded in his Diary: 'I visited with Sir Kenholm Digby with whom I had much discourse of chymical matters. I shew'd him a particular way of extracting oyle of [sulphur] & he gave me a certaine powder with which he affirm'd he had fixed [mercury] before the late King, which he advised me to try and digest a litlle better, & gave me a Water, which he said was... raine water of the Autumnal aequinox exceedingly rectified, very volatile, it had a tast of a strong vitriolique, and smelt like aquajortis, he intended it for a disolvant of [gold].' Betty Jo Dobbs, in Ambix (1973), identifies several items of significance in Evelyn's brief account: the 'free exchange of information and chemicals'; the reference to Digby having previously fixed mercury 'before the late King,' Charles I, who had been executed in January 1649; and the transparency of the chemical language, which 'is rational and refers to specific physical substances' rather than allegorical states of soul. Dobbs identifies the powder as possibly the same one described in Digby's posthumous Secrets (1682): 'A Process to fix [mercury of antimony], or the Common [mercury].' The Paris encounter illustrates the character of gentlemen's alchemical culture in the mid-seventeenth century: cooperative, technically specific, and oriented toward laboratory verification.
events.scholarly_grounding: Betty Jo Dobbs analyzed Evelyn's account of his Paris visit to Digby, drawing on Evelyn's Diary (ed. E. S. de Beer, 1955, III, 48), in 'Studies in the Natural Philosophy of Sir Kenelm Digby Part II: Digby and Alchemy' in Ambix vol. 20 no. 3 (1973) pp.143-163.

events.title: Digby Backs Hartlib's Universal Laboratory and General Chemical Council
events.description: During a temporary return to England in 1654, Sir Kenelm Digby met and immediately became an enthusiastic backer of Frederick Clodius, the son-in-law of Samuel Hartlib, who had recently established a laboratory in Hartlib's back-kitchen in London. Betty Jo Dobbs, in Ambix (1973), reconstructs the episode from Hartlib's letters to Robert Boyle: Hartlib reported that Digby had 'protested seriously... that in all his travels and converses with the choicest wits, both in Italy and France, he hath not met so much of theoretical solidity and practical dexterity both together, as he finds in my son [Clodius].' Digby's enthusiastic endorsement reinvigorated Hartlib's circle's pansophic project for a 'general chemical council' and a 'universal laboratory,' which was one of Hartlib's many schemes for state-supported institutional science. The timing was significant: Hartlib had by late 1653 given up hope in George Starkey, writing to Boyle that Starkey was 'altogether degenerated and hath, in a manner, undone himself and his family,' while Clodius was conducting experiments 'days and nights with no small success.' Digby's appearance in this context demonstrates both the network character of mid-century English chymical culture — in which Digby, Boyle, Starkey, Clodius, and Hartlib were all connected through the same correspondence circles — and the persistent aspiration for institutional organization of alchemical-chemical research that would eventually be realized through the Royal Society.
events.scholarly_grounding: Betty Jo Dobbs documented Digby's backing of the Hartlib universal laboratory scheme from Hartlib's letters to Boyle in 'Studies in the Natural Philosophy of Sir Kenelm Digby Part II: Digby and Alchemy' in Ambix vol. 20 no. 3 (1973) pp.143-163.
